pages.text:
Airbnb's AI-Native Transformation: Reading the AI-First Organization Through the CEO's Earnings Statements and the CTO's Testimony
Introduction: One year after saying Airbnb would become an "AI-first application," the company declared it had "rebuilt itself as an AI-native company."
On August 6, 2025, Airbnb co-founder and CEO Brian Chesky stated during an earnings call,
In the coming years, Airbnb will become an "AI-first application."
Airbnb beats on top and bottom lines for second quarter
Airbnb's revenue increased 13% from a year earlier, topping e
Airbnb, Inc. "Q2 2025 Earnings Call" Corrected Transcript
One year later, on August 6, 2026, Airbnb declared in its earnings announcement that it had fundamentally rebuilt Airbnb as an "AI-native company."
The conversation has shifted from the app to the nature of the company itself.
Airbnb reports Q2 2026 financial results.
"So, what is the AI-first organization that Airbnb is aiming for?"
The headline "AI wrote 60% of the code" does not answer this question.
While the 60% figure indicates a change in the volume of work, it does not explain who is doing what within the organization.
I interpret the basis for the AI-first organization Airbnb is aiming for by dividing it into two categories.
The first is the materials Airbnb has released to investors, such as earnings announcements, earnings calls, and filings with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC).
The second is the content shared by Ahmad Al-Dahle, who became CTO in January 2026, in an interview with AI-specialized media outlet Latent Space (published October 2, 2026).
Airbnb CTO Al-Dahle previously served as the head of generative AI at Meta and led the development of "Llama," the AI model that Meta released for anyone to use.
"Inside-Out AI: Rebuilding Airbnb Behind the Scenes and Across the Guest Experience"
The earnings materials show the results achieved in numbers, while the CTO's interview describes the target organizational image in words.
Notably, Latent Space has named Airbnb's approach "inside-out AI." This term is used by Latent Space and is not Airbnb's own terminology.
Inside-Out AI: Rebuilding Airbnb Behind the Scenes and Across the Guest Experience
After leading Meta’s Llama models, Ahmad Al-Dahle is now tran
Figure 1: Airbnb's earnings show the destination in numbers, while the CTO describes the target organizational image in words
Chapter 1: Airbnb handed over coding tasks and primary customer support to AI
First, I will list the milestones that can be confirmed in the earnings materials.
As of the first quarter of 2026, approximately 60% of the code generated by engineers at Airbnb is written in collaboration with AI.
CEO Chesky described this same figure as "written by AI" during the earnings call, adding that Airbnb estimates this to be roughly double the industry average.
The scope of this figure is "code generated by engineers," not the entirety of Airbnb's existing codebase.
Investing.com "Earnings call transcript: Airbnb Q1 2026 misses EPS but beats revenue"
The number of features and improvements released between January and June 2026 increased by approximately 80% compared to the same six-month period the previous year. For major initiatives, the time from conception to delivery was reduced by up to 60%.
For customer support, an AI assistant serves as the first point of contact for inquiries.
The percentage of consultations initiated by the AI assistant that were resolved without human intervention rose from approximately one-third in the October-December 2025 quarter to over 40% in the January-March 2026 quarter. By the April-June quarter, this reached approximately 45%, and the number of supported languages exceeded 50.
The denominator is "consultations initiated by the AI assistant," not all inquiries.
As of August 2025, this AI assistant was built by combining 13 models and fine-tuning them with tens of thousands of conversations.
Figure 2: Airbnb support features an AI assistant that responds first, while maintaining a path to human agents.
The change is also reflected in costs.
Support costs per booking in the April-June quarter fell by approximately 16% year-over-year. During the earnings call, CEO Chesky explained the reason, stating, "Part of it is due to improvements in the AI assistant."
Airbnb reports Q2 2026 financial results.
In the August 2026 earnings call, CFO Ellie Mertz stated that "the vast majority is due to AI agents."
The AI agents referred to here are the support AI assistants.
There is some variation in how management describes the reasons for the same figures.
Airbnb, Inc. "Q2 2026 Earnings Call" Corrected Transcript
The quarterly report (10-Q) filed with the SEC is a bit more specific.
In the April-June 2026 quarter, the use of AI in support reduced the number of inquiries handled by human agents, resulting in a $17 million reduction in costs paid to external contractors.
At Airbnb, much of the coding work and the initial response to inquiries have been handed over to AI.
What remains for engineers after coding work shifts to AI is covered in another article, so please refer to it below👇
Chapter 2: Airbnb changed its approach to giving small teams clear missions and releasing features as soon as they are ready.
CEO Chesky has repeatedly explained the methodology behind these numbers during earnings calls.
Give small, elite teams clear missions, release simple improvements to learn, and focus efforts on what works.
In the February 2026 earnings call, Chesky stated that he began this approach two years ago and expanded it company-wide after confirming it worked.
They have also stopped hoarding features for launch events, releasing them as soon as they are ready.
Regarding the performance for the April-June 2026 quarter, CEO Chesky stated that the reason was not a single product or initiative, but a combination of execution, talent, and an AI-accelerated approach.
Investing.com "Earnings call transcript: Airbnb Q1 2026 misses EPS but beats revenue"
Airbnb, Inc. "Q2 2026 Earnings Call" Corrected Transcript
Airbnb, Inc. "Q4 2025 Earnings Call" Corrected Transcript
CEO Chesky does not view the utilization rate of AI tools as a metric for success.
He called the figure that over 80% of engineers use AI tools a "vanity metric," stating that what matters is the company's culture and its ability to adapt to change.
Airbnb, Inc. "Q4 2025 Earnings Call" Corrected Transcript
The role of humans is also beginning to change.
CEO Chesky stated that Airbnb "must move at the speed of AI," indicating that management roles focused solely on overseeing people will not be as necessary as they once were. He also mentioned that design and engineering managers are returning to hands-on coding work.
Investing.com "Earnings call transcript: Airbnb Q1 2026 misses EPS but beats revenue"
CTO Al-Dahle goes even further.
He ended the practice of creating requirements documents and handing them off from designers to engineers, instead having planning, design, and development teams deliberate from the start using working prototypes.
Al-Dahle's belief is that companies organized by purpose and outcome, rather than by function, are stronger in the AI era.
However, regarding the future of team structure, Chesky himself stated that "it is too early to say." Organization by outcome is the CTO's policy and is not the final form of the company known as Airbnb.
What about the number of people? At the end of 2025, there were approximately 8,200 employees.
In the April-June 2026 quarter, personnel expenses in the operations and support departments increased by $27 million due to an increase in average headcount. The number of employees has not decreased.
Marts explains that because the output and speed obtained from current employees have increased significantly, there is no need to increase headcount as much as in the past.
Chapter 3: Airbnb has kept the judgment of complex and sensitive cases in the hands of employees
While there are tasks that Airbnb has handed over to AI, there are also judgments that have been left in human hands.
According to the annual report (10-K) filed with the SEC, as of the end of 2025, Airbnb has entrusted the majority of support inquiries to approximately 13,000 outsourced personnel. Internal support employees focus on complex and sensitive cases.
CEO Chesky called AI-based customer support the "hardest problem for AI." This is because incorrect answers are not permitted, and urgent cases or matters involving trust and safety must be accurately handed over to humans.
CTO Al-Dahle also says that they intentionally choose which cases to have AI solve and decide which cases not to leave to AI yet.
Even in the development field, a line is drawn between AI and humans.
According to CTO Al-Dahle, many teams have begun automating system monitoring and primary response to failures (on-call).
When a monitoring alert is triggered, an agent (a mechanism where AI proceeds with procedures on its own) is activated to determine whether it is a problem. If there is a problem, it issues a pull request (a proposal for code changes; hereafter PR), and an engineer reviews the PR.
If it is a false alarm, the agent closes the case itself.
Figure 3: A diagram of the flow where an agent determines Airbnb's on-call status and a human reviews the PR
The name of the figure above is "Handed over to agents," but CTO Al-Dahle's words are that many teams are "beginning" automation.
In the on-call flow, the initial determination of whether it is a problem is handled by an agent. What remains for humans is the judgment of whether or not to incorporate the PR proposed by the agent as code.
Figure 4: Airbnb separates where AI is entrusted with primary judgment and where humans make judgments
CEO Chesky also stated that regarding AI spending, he judges not by the amount of tokens (units of text processed by AI) used, but by how much product was released and the quality of the design.
It is also humans who decide not to make AI usage volume itself a goal.
Chapter 4: CTO Al-Dahle requires that even for PRs written by AI, the person who created them must explain them
What Airbnb leaves as a human role is not just judgment.
What CTO Al-Dahle strongly demands is that every engineer be able to explain what they created, even if it is a PR created by AI.
Inside-Out AI: Rebuilding Airbnb Behind the Scenes and Across the Guest Experience
After leading Meta’s Llama models, Ahmad Al-Dahle is now tran
Behind the above is a concern for young engineers.
Experienced engineers have acquired judgment through the experience of shipping systems, running them in production, and failing.
Now that AI handles many tasks, can young people gain the same experience?
Al-Dahle believes that if they continue to be required to explain things, young people can also learn interface design, the structure of the entire system, and the importance of testing.
"Inside-Out AI: Rebuilding Airbnb Behind the Scenes and Across the Guest Experience"
However, the policy of requiring the creator to explain is something that was mentioned in the CTO's interview.
I could not find any description to the same effect in the three earnings calls and earnings announcements I checked. Whether it is a rule of the company Airbnb or the CTO's policy cannot be distinguished from public documents.
The quality of AI output depends on the experience and judgment of the person using it.
How to pass on experience and judgment to the next generation is summarized in the following open-source book👇
Chapter 5: Airbnb is building up the context gained from previous services into the next ones
In May 2026, Airbnb expanded its services to include grocery delivery and airport transfers. In the August 2026 earnings call, CEO Chesky stated that newer services could be built faster than before, revealing that grocery delivery took 8–9 months to develop, while airport transfers took about 6 weeks.

Is Airbnb’s Dynamic Pricing Launch a Step Toward Becoming a Hotel-Like Franchisor?
Photo Credit: An Airbnb host in Kathmandu. Airbnb
In addition to dynamic pricing, Airbnb has floated the idea of adding more products and services for hosts, ranging from design services to financing. The soft franchise model might be more appropriate for individual hosts who don't require multi-platform distribution.
Airbnb’s new dynamic pricing tool is a first step toward becoming a “soft franchise” operator for hosts, similar to how big hotel groups like Hilton, Marriott, and IHG work with owners, according to a Bernstein research note.
Airbnb announced last month that it added dynamic pricing for hosts, who can tap on an Airbnb-recommended price range to view how their nightly rates would change based on supply and demand. This Airbnb service is currently free for hosts — although hosts pay around 15.5% commissions.
"The company is steadily expanding into areas that sit much closer to operating the asset itself. Pricing tools are the clearest example, but they are unlikely to be the last," Bernstein wrote.
Bernstein pointed to other potential offerings, such as revenue management, design consultation, property management software, guest communications, cleaning coordination, and insurance and smart-home hardware. "As each layer is added,

Tags: airbnb, airdna, casago, dynamic pricing, franchising, furnished finder, guesty, hotels, online travel newsletter, pricelabs, streamline, wheelhouse
Bernstein frames Airbnb's free dynamic pricing tool as the opening move toward a "soft franchise" model — operational support for hosts without the 10-20 year contracts or Airbnb branding of a hotel franchise.
Bernstein estimates dynamic pricing could eventually add 3-7% to Airbnb revenue, with more upside if Airbnb starts charging for it and competes directly with Wheelhouse, PriceLabs, and AirDNA.
Competitors and partners named the obstacle as distribution: hosts earn more across Vrbo, Booking.com, Expedia, and direct sites, and those rivals would have to let an Airbnb-owned operating layer connect.
Bernstein argues in a research note that Airbnb's new dynamic pricing tool is the first step toward the company operating as a "soft franchise" for hosts, closer to the way Hilton, Marriott, and IHG work with owners. Airbnb added the tool last month, letting hosts see how nightly rates would move with supply and demand. It is free today, on top of the roughly 15.5% commission hosts pay. Bernstein sees room for Airbnb to add revenue management, design consultation, property management software, guest communications, cleaning coordination, insurance, and smart-home hardware, which would shift the host relationship from transactional to operational. Bernstein estimates dynamic pricing alone could eventually lift Airbnb revenue 3-7%, with more upside if Airbnb charges for it as Wheelhouse, PriceLabs, and AirDNA do. Airbnb declined to comment. Partners and competitors were skeptical. Wheelhouse's Doug Truitt said hosts can't maximize revenue on a single platform, so Airbnb would need rivals including Vrbo, Booking.com, and Expedia to let it plug in. Furnished Finder CEO Jeff Hurst, a former Vrbo president, said Airbnb has more runway in guest services, including hotel stays, and that many hosts don't yet trust Airbnb enough to hand over operations.

Better Consumer Stock for 2026: Airbnb vs. DICK'S Sporting Goods
Airbnb maintains a dominant global marketplace with over 9 million active listings and a high net margin.
DICK'S Sporting Goods achieved significant revenue growth in FY 2025 while expanding its omnichannel retail presence.
Which of these consumer-facing giants is the better fit for your portfolio in 2026?
These 10 stocks could mint the next wave of millionaires ›
As global travel demand shifts and specialty retail adapts to new consumer habits, investors face a choice between two industry leaders. Should you buy Airbnb(NASDAQ:ABNB) or DICK'S Sporting Goods(NYSE:DKS)?
Airbnb transformed the travel landscape by connecting hosts and guests globally through its marketplace. DICK'S Sporting Goods has expanded its footprint through strategic acquisitions and a robust physical store network. Both companies cater to discretionary spending but offer vastly different business models, making this a classic match-up between technology and retail.
Airbnb operates as a global marketplace that connects travelers with hosts offering unique stays and experiences in over 220 countries and regions. By facilitating over 9 million active listings without owning the underlying real estate, the company maintains an asset-light model. This approach has allowed it to become a significant presence among travel and tourism stocks.
In its 2025 fiscal year (FY), revenue reached $12.3 billion, representing a growth rate of 10.8% compared to the previous year. This performance resulted in net income of $2.5 billion. The net margin of 20.4% remains high, although it is lower than the figures reported in the previous two fiscal years.
As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the company maintained a current ratio of 1.4x, indicating its ability to cover short-term liabilities with short-term assets. The debt-to-equity ratio was 0.3x, showing that total debt was low relative to shareholder equity. Free cash flow for FY 2025 reached $4.6 billion, though stock-based compensation (SBC) represented 34.3% of operating cash flow, which inflates reported cash generation since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.
DICK'S Sporting Goods serves a global sports community through banners like Golf Galaxy and its primary retail locations. A major part of its strategy involves a partnership with Nike(NYSE:NKE), which accounts for 31% of its consolidated merchandise purchases. Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk, though the company also works with partners like DoorDash(NASDAQ:DASH) and FedEx(NYSE:FDX) for fulfillment.
In FY 2025, revenue reached $17.2 billion, marking a significant growth rate of 28.1%. Despite this robust sales expansion, the company reported net income of $849.2 million. The net margin for the period was 4.9%, which is a decrease from the levels achieved in the prior two fiscal years.
As of its January 2026 balance sheet, the company reported a debt-to-equity ratio of 1.4x. This metric indicates that the company has $1.40 in total debt for every dollar of shareholder equity. The current ratio stood at 1.5x, while free cash flow for FY 2025 was $400.2 million.
Airbnb faces intense competition from established online travel agencies such as Booking Holdings(NASDAQ:BKNG) and Expedia Group(NASDAQ:EXPE). The company also deals with significant regulatory risks regarding short-term rental compliance and ongoing international tax disputes. Management must also navigate potential risks from AI development and operational hurdles related to global expansion.
DICK'S Sporting Goods operates in a fragmented retail market where it competes with other specialty shops. The company manages risks related to inventory shrink and its reliance on Nike, which provides a significant portion of its inventory. Furthermore, any failure to realize anticipated synergies from the Foot Locker acquisition or a decline in consumer spending could impact its long-term financial health.
DICK'S Sporting Goods appears significantly cheaper based on its Forward P/E, while Airbnb carries a premium price for its higher net margin and asset-light model. The P/S ratio measures market capitalization divided by sales over the past twelve months, while the Forward P/E compares the stock price to future earnings estimates.
Valuation metrics include sourcing from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.
Which stock would I buy in 2026?
Both Airbnb and DICK'S Sporting Goods possess compelling qualities that make them attractive stock investments. I like Airbnb's asset-light model. This allows the company to produce a high net income margin, which was 23% in the second quarter of 2026. That's why I bought shares in the lodging giant. However, its stock price has risen thanks to the travel industry's strong performance this year, making its valuation high.
DICK'S Sporting Goods was doing great until it released results for its fiscal Q2, ended Aug. 1. The company revealed its Foot Locker acquisition underperformed expectations, forcing management to reduce its 2026 full-year outlook. This caused the stock to crash. Shares fell 30% on Aug. 25, the day that earnings were released.
Interestingly, insiders quickly bought shares, suggesting the stock was undervalued at that point. Looking at its sales and forward earnings multiples, which are both near low points for the past year, indicate that shares appear cheap. This is why I would buy DICK'S stock over Airbnb. It has the potential to deliver a larger return than Airbnb right now.
Missed AI’s "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger
Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005.
But according to our analysts, we’re only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout, a massive technology build-out that Google’s CEO says could be more profound than fire or electricity.
While everyone watches the chip designers, one "backbone" company provides the critical technology that Nvidia and AMD literally cannot function without. We’ve detailed this under-the-radar player in our new AI Playbook.

pages.title: Up 10% in the Last Two Weeks, Is Airbnb the Perfect Stock for Today's Market? | The Motley Fool
pages.text:

Airbnb (ABNB +0.84%) has mostly been a disappointment for investors after initially surging out of the gate in its 2020 IPO, but in 2026, the stock is finally gaining momentum.
The #1 home-sharing platform has delivered better-than-expected growth, solid margins, and it's leveraging AI to improve user satisfaction. Meanwhile, it is expanding its platform with expanded experiences and guest services offerings.
Over the last two weeks, the stock is up 9.4%, even as the S&P 500 has fallen 1.6%, as the chart below shows.
Airbnb's gains have come as the tech sector has tumbled on concerns about an AI bubble and rising interest rates. However, the company has demonstrated its resilience and is well-positioned to thrive in such an environment. Here are three reasons why Airbnb is poised to be a winner in today's stock market.
Image source: Getty Images.
Stock investors generally dislike rising interest rates. After all, higher interest rates tend to make the bond market more attractive, leading investors to rotate out of stocks and into bonds. Additionally, higher interest rates put pressure on high-priced stocks like much of the tech sector, as it makes future earnings less valuable due to a higher discount rate in the discounted cash flow.
Normally, a company like Airbnb would be susceptible to that pressure, but the home-sharing leader actually earns significant profit from interest income thanks to the funds it holds in between customer bookings and disbursement. Through the first half of the year, it's earned $363 million in interest income, more than a third of its before-tax profit, and that number is likely to go up as interest rates go up. As of the end of the second quarter, the company held $12.2 billion in "funds receivable and amounts held on behalf of customers," on which it earns interest. That's a substantial advantage of its business model and gives it resilience when many of its tech stock peers are falling in the face of higher interest rates.
The launch of Meta Platforms' Muse also exposed a hidden advantage of Airbnb. Unlike its online travel agency (OTA) rivals Expedia and Booking, Airbnb's inventory is mostly specific to its platform. Expedia and Booking, on the other hand, are essentially middlemen, connecting users to hotels and acting as a clearinghouse for hotels that want to get their listings in front of prospective customers.
Tools like Muse make it easy for users to book directly with a given hotel or with the platform that offers the lowest price. It eliminates the friction that might ordinarily lead users to book directly on Expedia and Booking. Airbnb doesn't have this problem, as homestays don't typically offer the option of booking directly. That's one of the benefits Airbnb provides to its hosts, and it should give it an advantage if users continue to adopt AI agents.

3. The travel sector continues to outperform
While other discretionary sectors struggle, Airbnb and its travel stock peers have continued to deliver solid growth. Despite concerns about inflation, stock and home values remain at all-time highs, enabling wealthier people to spend on vacations and travel.
A number of other factors support that trend, including record wealth among the baby boomer generation and a preference for spending money on experiences over things among younger adults. Additionally, social media has helped stoke wanderlust, and the pandemic may have convinced people to travel while they have the opportunity.
Those tailwinds might not be permanent for Airbnb, but the current strength of the travel sector shows its advantages over other consumer-facing industries.
Taken together, those three factors make the stock a good bet to continue outperforming.

pages.title: Airbnb promised a refund for a noisy rental. Then it went quiet.
pages.text:
Tatsuyuki Morishita booked a “quiet” Airbnb in Toronto, only to be jolted awake by noise every night. An Airbnb agent promised a refund if he moved out early, but once he handed back the keys, the company tried to close the case with no refund. Can Morishita get Airbnb to honor its word?
PUBLISHED: October 19, 2026 at 6:30 AM PDT | UPDATED: October 19, 2026 at 12:46 PM PDT
Getting your Trinity Audio player ready...
Q: I booked an Airbnb rental in Toronto for a stay of more than two months. The listing description used the words “quiet” and “peaceful” five times, which was exactly what I needed for my stay.
Unfortunately, the reality was anything but calm. Almost every night, recurring heavy impact noise from the unit above would wake us up at 4 a.m. I didn’t just complain; I documented the disturbance with video and audio recordings. I shared these with the host multiple times, and while they acknowledged the ongoing noise, they couldn’t stop it.
I also reported the issue to Airbnb within the required 72-hour window. An agent reviewed my evidence and confirmed I was covered by Airbnb’s AirCover guarantee. He gave me a written commitment for a full refund of 12 unused nights and a 30% refund for the 20 nights we endured the noise. He even told me he was “currently processing” the request.
Since we moved out, Airbnb reassigned the file to multiple agents who all contradicted each other. One agent denied our eligibility entirely. Another senior manager claimed the host wasn’t willing to alter the dates, despite the thread showing the host had already approved the early checkout. The agent then tried to close the case without giving us a cent.
I just want Airbnb to honor the written commitment its agent made. Can you help me get them to pay what they promised?
— Tatsuyuki Morishita, North York, Ontario
A: Airbnb should have stuck to its word. When an agent confirms AirCover eligibility and provides a specific refund amount in writing, that’s a contract. You relied on that commitment when you packed your bags and left. For the company to play “hot potato” with your case afterward is unacceptable.
AirCover is supposed to protect guests when a listing isn’t what was advertised. Since “quiet” was a central feature of the description, the early-morning noise brigade was a clear violation.
You documented the noise, notified the host and got a promise from support before you left the premises. Good job! Many travelers make the mistake of leaving first and asking for money later, but you had the “green light” in writing.
When a company goes silent or starts walking back a promise, you should appeal to an executive. I list the names and email addresses of Airbnb’s leadership on my advocacy site, Elliott.org.
I contacted Airbnb on your behalf. Shortly after that, a member of the senior support team called you. While you rightly insisted on keeping the conversation in writing, they followed up on the platform to apologize. Airbnb honored the original refund of $1,268 and even threw in a $250 coupon for the trouble.
Christopher Elliott is the founder of Elliott Advocacy, a nonprofit organization that helps consumers solve their problems. Email him at chris@elliott.org or get help by contacting him on his site, Elliott.org.

pages.title: Utah police raided an Airbnb with guns drawn over stolen Legos, found nothing — and taxpayers will pay for it
pages.text:

Utah police raided an Airbnb with guns drawn over stolen Legos, found nothing — and taxpayers will pay for it
Mon, October 19, 2026 at 5:00 PM CDT 6 min read
gettyimages.com / Michael Blackshire (left); youtube.com / Reckless Ben (right)
On March 11, 2026, Utah cops with guns drawn, including an assault rifle, made their way into an Airbnb, executing a search warrant for "stolen Legos." They detained all of the occupants, including a 16-year-old minor, and took them down to the American Fork Police Department (AFPD) station for questioning. The cops found no stolen Legos, drugs or weapons in the Airbnb.
"This is how people can end up getting killed," attorney Solomon Radner said in a press conference. "This is not how a search warrant is supposed to go down, especially if you're dealing with people whose only crime, supposedly, is stolen Legos."

About seven months later, four of the arrested occupants — Sheldon Norcross, Tyler Shaw, Sierra Lauts and Steven Allen — filed a federal civil rights lawsuit against the city of American Fork and 13 of its police officers, according to a report by The Salt Lake Tribune. They alleged that their First and Fourth Amendment rights were violated during the encounter, according to local news outlet KSL.
The lawsuit included 19 counts that were supported by incriminating records taken from the officers' equipment –– including bodycam and dashcam footage. The plaintiffs, in the opinion of their legal counsel, were repeatedly targeted by American Fork officers without legal justification.
During one roadside stop before the Airbnb arrests, one officer was caught on camera saying, "I was gonna scare him a little bit and let him go, is all I really was gonna do."
While the lawsuit against American Fork is just beginning, much of the actual dispute that started everything has been settled. Because of the nature of the lawsuit, however, if the city loses or settles, the local taxpayers will be the ones who foot the bill.
The Lego collection that led to an armed raid and arrests
The story began with a prized Star Wars Lego collection that belonged to an elderly Oregon man, Ed Mansell, and his son Bryan. They had consigned the collection — which is allegedly worth $80,000, including an ultra-rare Cloud City set valued as high as $10,000 — at an Oregon store branch of Bricks & Minifigs.
The collection vanished between corporate transfers and ownership changes, leaving the family unpaid, according to Courthouse News.
In a bid to recover their collection, the family reached out to Ben Schneider, a Los Angeles YouTuber known as Reckless Ben, whose channel digs into disputes like this one. He offered to help and, together with some local helpers, traveled to American Fork to film a documentary, file lawsuits and serve court papers to an individual connected to the missing Legos.
Schneider, who has 2.6 million YouTube subscribers, posted a video called "I tracked down the thief who stole $200,000 of LEGO."
But Schneider and his helpers ended up with four days of traffic stops, searches and, finally, the raid that landed them all in police questioning.
While none of the four individuals who filed the civil rights lawsuit were ever charged with any crime, Schneider himself faced criminal charges for stalking and residential picketing, according to a news report by ABC4 Utah.
Read More: Vanguard reveals what's coming for U.S. stocks — and it could be bad news for this group of investors
Why taxpayers cover the bill in cases like this
Federal civil rights lawsuits, like the one in this story, run on a federal law known as Section 1983, which lets people sue government officials, including police officers, who violate their constitutional rights.
However, there is a Qualified Immunity that shields government officials from being sued individually for money damages in civil court — and if a judge grants an officer Qualified Immunity early in a lawsuit, the case against that specific officer is completely dismissed.
This may not be the case for the Utah officers in this story.
American Fork Police Chief Cameron Paul publicly admitted the department made errors regarding the warrant affidavit, saying "we didn't do this perfectly" and "several issues weren't handled well, or were handled outside of policy," ABC4.com reported.
Because the chief admitted to procedural errors and officers were recorded admitting intent to scare citizens, the city faces significant legal exposure.
If the court finds the officers acted with reckless disregard for constitutional rights, Qualified Immunity may be stripped.
However, even if an officer loses Qualified Immunity, goes to trial and loses the civil lawsuit, they still rarely pay a dime. This is due to a process called indemnification.
Ultimately, the money used to pay the victims of police misconduct comes out of the city's budget or insurance policies funded by taxpayers, not the individual officer's bank account.
What the Mansell family has recovered so far
According to a Central Oregon Daily article, on Aug. 19, Bricks & Minifigs announced a "comprehensive and amicable resolution of a private civil dispute" with the Mansell family, compensating them with an undisclosed amount and issuing an "unqualified apology."
It stressed the deal was "a compromise of disputed claims, not an admission of liability or wrongdoing."
Bryan Mansell releases all claims against Bricks & Minifigs, which in turn drops its suit against him — but the lawsuits against Reckless Ben still remain active.
A GoFundMe set up by Schneider for Mansell has raised $531,411 of a $550,000 target at the time of writing.

Advance Auto Parts focuses on the essential automotive repair market through a vast physical network. Airbnb operates a capital-light digital platform that revolutionized the hospitality industry. Advance Auto Parts operates as a major provider in the automotive aftermarket, selling parts and accessories to a diverse customer base. The company splits its business between professional installers and do-it-yourself (DIY) customers, with professional sales accounting for approximately 50% of revenue in 2025. It remains a fixture among retail stocks by operating 4,311 stores and supporting nearly 800 independently owned Carquest locations. In January 2026, the company expanded its private-label offerings by launching Argos, a brand designed to capture value-conscious shoppers.
Financial performance has faced headwinds recently as the company navigates a changing retail landscape. According to its latest annual report filed for FY 2025, revenue reached about $8.6 billion, representing a decrease of approximately 5.4% compared to the prior year. Despite the dip in sales, the company reported net income of roughly $44 million for the period. This resulted in a net margin, which measures the percentage of revenue kept as profit, of approximately 0.5%.
As of its January 2026 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was roughly 2.4x. This ratio measures financial leverage by comparing total debt to shareholder equity. Its current ratio, which indicates how easily a company can pay its short-term bills using its assets, stood at approximately 1.7x. Free cash flow for the fiscal year was negative, at minus-$298.0 million. Free cash flow equals cash flow from operations minus capital expenditures and represents the cash a business generates after accounting for investments in its physical assets.
Airbnb manages a global marketplace that connects hosts with travelers seeking unique stays and experiences. The company does not own the properties listed; instead, it provides the digital infrastructure for more than 5 million hosts to list their homes. This capital-light model allows the platform to scale rapidly across 220 countries and regions. By focusing on a two-sided network, the company benefits from a self-sustaining cycle where more hosts attract more guests, and vice versa.
Growth remains a central theme for the travel leader as it expands its international footprint. In FY 2025, revenue reached about $12.3 billion, which indicates a growth rate of approximately 10.3% over the previous year. The company reported net income of roughly $2.5 billion for the same period. This led to a net margin of approximately 20.4%, showing that the company retains a significant portion of its sales as profit after all expenses are paid.
As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was approximately 0.3x. This indicates a conservative level of debt relative to equity. Its current ratio was roughly 1.4x, suggesting the company maintains sufficient liquidity to meet its near-term obligations. Free cash flow reached nearly $4.6 billion in FY 2025. Note that stock-based compensation (SBC) represented roughly 34% of operating cash flow, which inflates reported cash generation since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.
Advance Auto Parts faces significant competitive threats from national automotive retailers like AutoZone Inc. (AZO +2.01%) and O'Reilly Automotive Inc. (ORLY +1.07%), as well as mass merchandisers like Amazon.com Inc. (AMZN +0.07%). The company is currently exposed to operational risks from its ongoing restructuring efforts, including potential costs from lease terminations and store closures. Furthermore, cybersecurity remains a concern following a previous data breach settlement, while global logistics disruptions and trade tariffs could impact its supply chain stability.
Airbnb is subject to high competitive pressure in the travel industry from search engines and hotel chains, as well as online travel agencies like Booking Holdings Inc. (BKNG +0.81%). The platform faces ongoing regulatory risks as various local and international governments implement short-term rental bans or restrictions. Additionally, the company is exposed to financial risks from its dependence on cloud hosting infrastructure and ongoing legal disputes with tax authorities regarding the valuation of its intellectual property.
Airbnb carries a much higher valuation reflecting its double-digit growth, while Advance Auto Parts trades at a deep discount amid its business turnaround.
Valuation metrics include those sourced from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from those of other data providers.
Which stock would I buy in 2026?
Advance Auto Parts is in the midst of turning around the struggles it has experienced over the past few years around sales growth, margins, and market share. The aftermarket auto parts business has been in a slump, due largely to a mix of factors: weak do-it-yourselfer demand, vehicle electrification, intense competition, and general pocketbook pressures on consumers.
Company management has been addressing the business' issues by rolling out a new multi-year turnaround program. That started in late 2024, including closing stores, optimizing store footprints, and overhauling its supply chain. To date, the program has produced mixed results. First-quarter fiscal 2026 results that were much better than expected, with revenue of $2.6 billion and net income of $25 million. But the second quarter disappointed the street, and shares plunged as revenue fell short of consensus at $2 billion, even as net income and other metrics beat expectations.
Analysts see full-year 2026 sales a little lower at $8.57 billion, with net income improving to $167 million, roughly four times 2025.
Airbnb reported an excellent second quarter of fiscal 2026, rallying shares sharply after results. The business beat consensus revenue estimates by $100 million, reporting $3.6 billion in sales, up 17% from the same period in 2025, driven by a strong increase in booked nights. Foreign markets like India and Latin America, two markets in which Airbnb is seeking growth, were exceptionally strong. The third quarter should see sales close to $4.8 billion and net income around $1.7 billion.
The business is finding ways to expand its popular travel business, embracing features like buy now, pay later (BNPL) on reservations, a form of short-term lending. The network advantage of Airbnb's history, over 2 billion guest arrivals since 2008, and the lack of host presence on AI (meaning a competitor using AI has little data and information to scrape in order to form a competing product) give it a competitive moat.
For the full year, management expects sales of $14.1 billion with net income of $3.2 billion.
So which stock to choose? In the highly competitive retail sector, Advance Auto Parts is by no means guaranteed success despite its strong efforts to recover. Airbnb's capital-light model also means it has far fewer competitive moats. But it's the healthier and faster-growing business of the two, and until the company can't execute and competitors catch up, it appears to be a long-term buy.

pages.title: Better Consumer Stock for 2026: Airbnb vs. DICK'S Sporting Goods | The Motley Fool
pages.text:
▲ S&P 500 +---%|▲ Stock Advisor +---%Join The Motley Fool
As global travel demand shifts and specialty retail adapts to new consumer habits, investors face a choice between two industry leaders. Should you buy Airbnb (ABNB +0.84%) or DICK'S Sporting Goods (DKS -0.48%)?
Airbnb transformed the travel landscape by connecting hosts and guests globally through its marketplace. DICK'S Sporting Goods has expanded its footprint through strategic acquisitions and a robust physical store network. Both companies cater to discretionary spending but offer vastly different business models, making this a classic match-up between technology and retail.
Airbnb operates as a global marketplace that connects travelers with hosts offering unique stays and experiences in over 220 countries and regions. By facilitating over 9 million active listings without owning the underlying real estate, the company maintains an asset-light model. This approach has allowed it to become a significant presence among travel and tourism stocks.
In its 2025 fiscal year (FY), revenue reached $12.3 billion, representing a growth rate of 10.8% compared to the previous year. This performance resulted in net income of $2.5 billion. The net margin of 20.4% remains high, although it is lower than the figures reported in the previous two fiscal years.
As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the company maintained a current ratio of 1.4x, indicating its ability to cover short-term liabilities with short-term assets. The debt-to-equity ratio was 0.3x, showing that total debt was low relative to shareholder equity. Free cash flow for FY 2025 reached $4.6 billion, though stock-based compensation (SBC) represented 34.3% of operating cash flow, which inflates reported cash generation since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.
DICK'S Sporting Goods serves a global sports community through banners like Golf Galaxy and its primary retail locations. A major part of its strategy involves a partnership with Nike (NKE +1.80%), which accounts for 31% of its consolidated merchandise purchases. Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk, though the company also works with partners like DoorDash (DASH -0.96%) and FedEx (FDX +1.70%) for fulfillment.
In FY 2025, revenue reached $17.2 billion, marking a significant growth rate of 28.1%. Despite this robust sales expansion, the company reported net income of $849.2 million. The net margin for the period was 4.9%, which is a decrease from the levels achieved in the prior two fiscal years.
As of its January 2026 balance sheet, the company reported a debt-to-equity ratio of 1.4x. This metric indicates that the company has $1.40 in total debt for every dollar of shareholder equity. The current ratio stood at 1.5x, while free cash flow for FY 2025 was $400.2 million.
Airbnb faces intense competition from established online travel agencies such as Booking Holdings (BKNG +0.81%) and Expedia Group (EXPE +3.10%). The company also deals with significant regulatory risks regarding short-term rental compliance and ongoing international tax disputes. Management must also navigate potential risks from AI development and operational hurdles related to global expansion.
DICK'S Sporting Goods operates in a fragmented retail market where it competes with other specialty shops. The company manages risks related to inventory shrink and its reliance on Nike, which provides a significant portion of its inventory. Furthermore, any failure to realize anticipated synergies from the Foot Locker acquisition or a decline in consumer spending could impact its long-term financial health.
DICK'S Sporting Goods appears significantly cheaper based on its Forward P/E, while Airbnb carries a premium price for its higher net margin and asset-light model. The P/S ratio measures market capitalization divided by sales over the past twelve months, while the Forward P/E compares the stock price to future earnings estimates.
Valuation metrics include sourcing from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.
Which stock would I buy in 2026?
Both Airbnb and DICK'S Sporting Goods possess compelling qualities that make them attractive stock investments. I like Airbnb's asset-light model. This allows the company to produce a high net income margin, which was 23% in the second quarter of 2026. That's why I bought shares in the lodging giant. However, its stock price has risen thanks to the travel industry's strong performance this year, making its valuation high.
DICK'S Sporting Goods was doing great until it released results for its fiscal Q2, ended Aug. 1. The company revealed its Foot Locker acquisition underperformed expectations, forcing management to reduce its 2026 full-year outlook. This caused the stock to crash. Shares fell 30% on Aug. 25, the day that earnings were released.
Interestingly, insiders quickly bought shares, suggesting the stock was undervalued at that point. Looking at its sales and forward earnings multiples, which are both near low points for the past year, indicate that shares appear cheap. This is why I would buy DICK'S stock over Airbnb. It has the potential to deliver a larger return than Airbnb right now.

Airbnb (ABNB) put its fall product update front and center this week, spotlighting AI-powered search and new on-trip services that tighten the link between its travel platform and day-to-day trip logistics.
Recent price action has been broadly supportive of that story, with a 30.59% year to date share price return and a 37.96% total shareholder return over the past year, suggesting that momentum has been building as Airbnb rolls out product upgrades and investors reassess its risk and growth profile.
See how Airbnb's AI-driven travel push fits alongside other fast-moving consumer services by reviewing our hand-picked list of 20 high quality undiscovered gems with strong fundamentals and room for a rerating.
Airbnb now trades close to analyst targets, yet internal fair value estimates still suggest a sizable gap. Is this latest AI-fueled rally already pricing in the story, or is that 40% implied discount too wide?
Most Popular Narrative: 4.5% Undervalued
Airbnb's most followed valuation storyline pegs fair value at $181.84 per share compared with the recent $173.70 close. This points to a modest upside gap that still needs to be justified by the underlying business mix and product momentum.
"This is the first time in a while where Airbnb is not asking investors to believe that the next growth engine is coming. Some of it is actually showing up. Core markets are accelerating again. International markets are still growing quickly. AI is reducing costs. The core product is converting better. Hotels are gaining traction. Experiences are at least moving in the right direction. And profitability remains very strong."
See why 86 investors see Airbnb as 4% undervalued.
According to TickerTickle, that fair value view rests on a few key levers. The narrative uses a 12% annual revenue growth rate, a 24.5% long term net margin and a future P/E of 27x, all discounted at 8.5%. Those inputs combine into a fair value estimate of $181.84, only slightly above the current share price yet still meaningfully below the $290.97 future cash flow value implied by the SWS DCF model.
This creates an interesting split for readers. The DCF output and Simply Wall St valuation checks flag Airbnb as trading 40.3% below future cash flow value. The popular narrative frames the gap as a 4.5% discount to fair value. That tension often reflects different expectations for how quickly earnings and free cash flow convert into shareholder returns, rather than a disagreement about the direction of the business itself.
For now, the story that markets seem to be responding to is clear. Airbnb has become profitable, is generating high quality earnings, carries a high 34.5% forecast return on equity in three years and has been using strong free cash flow to fund buybacks and reduce share count. At the same time, earnings are projected to grow 15.55% per year, which is slightly slower than the broader US market, so investors still need to decide how much to pay for that mix of quality and growth.

Still, tighter regulations in key regions and the unresolved US$1.3b IRS dispute could quickly change how investors view Airbnb's earnings power and valuation story.

Airbnb might look cheap on future cash flows, but its P/E of 38.1x tells a different story. That multiple is above the US Hospitality group at 19.6x and ahead of the 30.5x peer average. It also sits above a 30x fair ratio, which raises clear valuation risk for anyone buying on earnings multiples alone.

Airbnb recently rolled out a fall product update that connects travelers with friends' trips, introduces AI-powered search, and adds on-trip services like Instacart grocery delivery, laundry, baby gear rentals, and local experiences.
The tighter integration of AI search with services such as grocery and gear delivery points to Airbnb pushing deeper into higher-fee, non-lodging spend across each trip.
We will now look at how Airbnb's investment narrative is shaped by these AI-powered search upgrades and expanded on-trip services.

To own Airbnb, you have to believe it can keep turning a global host network, strong direct traffic, and an expanding services layer into consistent earnings while staying ahead of new AI booking agents and regulation. The fall product update sits right on that thesis. It tightens the link between discovery, booking, and on-trip spend, but does not change the core near term driver, which is execution on the broader travel platform vision.
The biggest short term swing factor is how effectively Airbnb can grow higher fee experiences, hotels, and services without eroding guest or host satisfaction. The main risk remains external pressure, from AI intermediaries that could sit between Airbnb and users, and from city level rules that may limit supply. The new features are helpful but not decisive against either issue yet.
The most relevant piece of the recent rollout is the AI powered search that lets you describe a trip in natural language and see homes, experiences, and services in one view. For investors, this speaks directly to two things that matter for Airbnb: how efficiently the marketplace matches supply and demand, and how much of a trip's wallet the platform can realistically capture.
Execution is what counts. If AI summaries and side by side comparisons reduce search friction, guests may be more willing to book longer stays, try hotels on Airbnb, or attach services like grocery delivery and laundry. That supports the existing catalyst around experiences and services raising revenue per booking, but it also raises the bar on product quality. Any mismatch between AI recommendations, actual listings, and on trip services would quickly show up in reviews and support costs.
Airbnb's narrative projects US$18.6b revenue and US$4.7b earnings by 2029. That path assumes revenue growing at 12.3% per year and an earnings increase of about US$2b from US$2.7b today.

Airbnb's AI update tests the "full travel platform" story
The Airbnb Narrative hinges on whether it can turn an accommodation app into a broader travel and living platform, with AI as the connective tissue. This product update goes straight at that premise because it links search, group planning and on-trip services inside one funnel.
"Integration of homes, hotels, experiences and new services on a single Airbnb platform, supported by hotels reportedly growing about 3x as fast as homes and a meaningful share of first time hotel guests later booking homes, can expand total booking volume and support higher long term revenue and earnings power..."

The flip side is competitive pressure. Google, Booking Holdings and emerging AI booking agents all want to own the customer relationship, not just the transaction. By pulling social trip planning, history from friends and on-trip logistics into its own app, Airbnb is effectively trying to reduce the risk analysts flagged around third party AI agents diluting direct traffic.
For investors, this product news only really matters in the context of whether they believe the longer term story about Airbnb becoming a multi-vertical travel platform powered by AI, not just a better search bar for holiday rentals.

Fri, October 16, 2026 at 4:00 PM CDT 5 min read
Brian Chesky, 45, the CEO of San Francisco-based home-sharing company Airbnb, [NASDAQ:ABNB] has pretty much given up on writing emails. He still answers the ones that land in his inbox, but when he needs something from his team, he picks up his phone and texts them instead.
"I don't know if I write an email a week," Chesky said in an interview with Time. Texts are a different story, he explained, because, "When you get a text message, it doesn't feel like work to respond."
Jeff Bezos backs a platform that lets anyone invest in rental homes for as little as $100 — 6 ways to build wealth like a landlord without actually being one
A single line on your car insurance policy could be inflating your premium by up to 30% — here's what to change
Dave Ramsey warns nearly 50% of Americans are making 1 big Social Security mistake. Here's what it is and 3 simple steps to fix it ASAP
Among big-company CEOs who've talked publicly about how they communicate, he's in the minority. Nvidia's Jensen Huang and Uber's Dara Khosrowshahi, for example, still do a lot of their managing over email.
Most office workers couldn't skip email if they tried, since Microsoft 365 users get 117 emails a day on average and give most of them less than a minute, according to a report published June by Microsoft.
Chesky told Time that if he had to rank how he likes to communicate, face-to-face conversations would come first, then Zoom, then texting, with email likely in last place. Emails start with a subject line, he pointed out, whereas a text goes straight to someone.
When something needs fixing, he'd rather sit down with the person, call them or fire off a text than open his inbox.
Read More: Vanguard reveals what's coming for U.S. stocks — and it could be bad news for this group of investors
Which CEOs still run their companies by email?
Then there's Huang, 63, CEO of chipmaker Nvidia [NASDAQ:NVDA], who works almost the opposite way. Nvidia staff have long emailed him short notes known inside the company as "Top-5 Things" — each a rundown of what they're working on and noticing. He goes through those notes daily to catch early hints of where the business is heading, The Wall Street Journal reported in December, 2024.
Over at ride-hailing company Uber [NYSE:UBER], CEO Dara Khosrowshahi, 57, wants his staff to answer emails on weekends. On a Feb. 23 episode of The Diary of a CEO, he said anyone who doesn't answer his Saturday email can expect a pointed follow-up from him on Sunday.
Late-night work is creeping up for everyone else, too. The number of meetings kicking off after 8 p.m. rose 16% in a year, according to Microsoft's report, and a typical employee now trades more than 50 messages outside the 9-to-5.
In Microsoft's 2025 Work Trend Index survey of 31,000 knowledge workers across 31 markets, 48% of employees and 52% of leaders said their work feels "chaotic and fragmented."
How to reach a boss who barely uses email
You can simply ask your manager (maybe during your next one-on-one) where they prefer to read work messages, whether that's email, Slack, Teams, or even texts.
And for anything important, it helps to cover your bases. Any serious communication should be in writing. That would include things like a raise request, a change in your duties, or a deadline you want on record. But there's no harm in sending a quick text to let your boss know it's there. And if you need an answer within the hour, a call or a text is probably your best bet, since that's how Chesky deals with his own urgent problems.
It also pays to find out what your boss expects after hours, because being reachable all the time can wear you down. In a June 2026 analysis, Eurofound, the Dublin-based EU agency that studies working conditions, found that stress at work climbs with how often people are contacted outside their hours. Among workers across the European Union who get contacted every day after hours, 59% say they feel stress at work always or almost always. That falls to 17% among those who are never contacted. The figures come from the agency's 2024 European Working Conditions Survey.
Interestingly enough, managers are more likely than any other group of workers to get those after-hours messages, according to Eurofound.
Chesky, for his part, says he tries not to text people he believes are spending time with family, emergencies aside. If your boss has never said whether they follow a similar rule, it's a fair question to bring up.

What Changed In Airbnb's Story?
Tue, October 20, 2026 at 3:23 PM CDT 3 min read
Airbnb (ABNB) stock trades at 38.6 times earnings, against 22.9 for the S&P 500. Shareholders paying that much need to know what they are buying, but there is a twist: what management talks up on its calls has changed. During the fiscal Q3 2024 call, management said it was focused on making hosting just as popular as traveling on Airbnb, which means getting more people to rent out their homes. On the latest call, management made the case for something else. So what is it?
During the fiscal Q2 2026 call in August, management highlighted hotels, saying hotel nights are growing about three times faster than the homes business. The company also described the next stage for Airbnb as a one-stop shop for travel, and said it had expanded Airbnb Services into grocery delivery, car rental, airport pickup and luggage storage.
Before that, hosts were the supply story. Management introduced co-host networks on the fiscal Q3 2024 call as an easy way for a homeowner to find a local host to run the listing. By the fiscal Q2 2025 call, management said 100,000 listings were managed by co-hosts and that the program could lead to millions more homes on Airbnb. Co-hosts did not come up on the latest call, and hotels took the spotlight. Homes still got attention: management said more than 150,000 homes in World Cup host cities were listed on Airbnb for the first time.
How Big Are Hotels Next To Airbnb's Homes?
Hotels still represent a small part of Airbnb. Management said on the fiscal Q2 2026 call that they account for a single-digit percentage of nights booked. As a result, homes still make up the great bulk of what guests book, even with hotel nights growing about three times as fast.
Management said nights and seats booked grew 10% from a year earlier, accelerating from fiscal Q1 2026. Revenue grew 16.5% in fiscal Q2 2026, faster than the 12.7% growth in fiscal Q2 2025.
Should Airbnb Holders Worry About Its Push Into Hotels?
So far the push reads as more reassuring than concerning, because Airbnb as a whole is growing faster, not slower. Revenue over the twelve months to June 2026 grew 13.6%, against 10.2% for the twelve months before. Management also said roughly 35% of first-time hotel guests return to Airbnb to book a home, meaning hotels appear to be bringing new guests to the homes side.
The concern is not hotels, but the supply of homes. In September, the EU set out plans to give European cities more leeway to curb short-term rentals such as Airbnb. On the August call, before those plans came out, management said policy is a risk, but not an existential one.
When Airbnb reports on or around November 5, 2026, the measure to watch is growth in nights and seats booked. Management expects growth at a low double-digit rate for fiscal Q3 2026.
How To Act On ABNB?
Not necessarily on Airbnb alone, if your goal is long-term wealth. Wealth is built by owning the companies that keep outperforming, the leaders of their industries, wherever they are. Here are two companies from Airbnb's own industry that have beaten it. Over the five years to October 2026, Booking Holdings stock rose 69% and Royal Caribbean stock rose 245%, while Airbnb stock rose 2.8%.

Introduction: One year after saying Airbnb would become an "AI-first application," the company declared it had "rebuilt itself as an AI-native company."
On August 6, 2025, Airbnb co-founder and CEO Brian Chesky stated during an earnings call,
In the coming years, Airbnb will become an "AI-first application."

Airbnb, Inc. "Q2 2025 Earnings Call" Corrected Transcript
One year later, on August 6, 2026, Airbnb declared in its earnings announcement that it had fundamentally rebuilt Airbnb as an "AI-native company."
The conversation has shifted from the app to the nature of the company itself.
Airbnb reports Q2 2026 financial results.
"So, what is the AI-first organization that Airbnb is aiming for?"
The headline "AI wrote 60% of the code" does not answer this question.
While the 60% figure indicates a change in the volume of work, it does not explain who is doing what within the organization.
I interpret the basis for the AI-first organization Airbnb is aiming for by dividing it into two categories.
The first is the materials Airbnb has released to investors, such as earnings announcements, earnings calls, and filings with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC).
The second is the content shared by Ahmad Al-Dahle, who became CTO in January 2026, in an interview with AI-specialized media outlet Latent Space (published October 2, 2026).
Airbnb CTO Al-Dahle previously served as the head of generative AI at Meta and led the development of "Llama," the AI model that Meta released for anyone to use.
"Inside-Out AI: Rebuilding Airbnb Behind the Scenes and Across the Guest Experience"
The earnings materials show the results achieved in numbers, while the CTO's interview describes the target organizational image in words.
Notably, Latent Space has named Airbnb's approach "inside-out AI." This term is used by Latent Space and is not Airbnb's own terminology.
Inside-Out AI: Rebuilding Airbnb Behind the Scenes and Across the Guest Experience
After leading Meta’s Llama models, Ahmad Al-Dahle is now tran
Figure 1: Airbnb's earnings show the destination in numbers, while the CTO describes the target organizational image in words
Chapter 1: Airbnb handed over coding tasks and primary customer support to AI
First, I will list the milestones that can be confirmed in the earnings materials.
As of the first quarter of 2026, approximately 60% of the code generated by engineers at Airbnb is written in collaboration with AI.
CEO Chesky described this same figure as "written by AI" during the earnings call, adding that Airbnb estimates this to be roughly double the industry average.
The scope of this figure is "code generated by engineers," not the entirety of Airbnb's existing codebase.
Investing.com "Earnings call transcript: Airbnb Q1 2026 misses EPS but beats revenue"
The number of features and improvements released between January and June 2026 increased by approximately 80% compared to the same six-month period the previous year. For major initiatives, the time from conception to delivery was reduced by up to 60%.
For customer support, an AI assistant serves as the first point of contact for inquiries.
The percentage of consultations initiated by the AI assistant that were resolved without human intervention rose from approximately one-third in the October-December 2025 quarter to over 40% in the January-March 2026 quarter. By the April-June quarter, this reached approximately 45%, and the number of supported languages exceeded 50.
The denominator is "consultations initiated by the AI assistant," not all inquiries.
As of August 2025, this AI assistant was built by combining 13 models and fine-tuning them with tens of thousands of conversations.
Figure 2: Airbnb support features an AI assistant that responds first, while maintaining a path to human agents.
The change is also reflected in costs.
Support costs per booking in the April-June quarter fell by approximately 16% year-over-year. During the earnings call, CEO Chesky explained the reason, stating, "Part of it is due to improvements in the AI assistant."
Airbnb reports Q2 2026 financial results.
In the August 2026 earnings call, CFO Ellie Mertz stated that "the vast majority is due to AI agents."
The AI agents referred to here are the support AI assistants.
There is some variation in how management describes the reasons for the same figures.
Airbnb, Inc. "Q2 2026 Earnings Call" Corrected Transcript
The quarterly report (10-Q) filed with the SEC is a bit more specific.
In the April-June 2026 quarter, the use of AI in support reduced the number of inquiries handled by human agents, resulting in a $17 million reduction in costs paid to external contractors.
At Airbnb, much of the coding work and the initial response to inquiries have been handed over to AI.
What remains for engineers after coding work shifts to AI is covered in another article, so please refer to it below👇
Chapter 2: Airbnb changed its approach to giving small teams clear missions and releasing features as soon as they are ready.
CEO Chesky has repeatedly explained the methodology behind these numbers during earnings calls.
Give small, elite teams clear missions, release simple improvements to learn, and focus efforts on what works.
In the February 2026 earnings call, Chesky stated that he began this approach two years ago and expanded it company-wide after confirming it worked.
They have also stopped hoarding features for launch events, releasing them as soon as they are ready.
Regarding the performance for the April-June 2026 quarter, CEO Chesky stated that the reason was not a single product or initiative, but a combination of execution, talent, and an AI-accelerated approach.
Investing.com "Earnings call transcript: Airbnb Q1 2026 misses EPS but beats revenue"
Airbnb, Inc. "Q2 2026 Earnings Call" Corrected Transcript
Airbnb, Inc. "Q4 2025 Earnings Call" Corrected Transcript
CEO Chesky does not view the utilization rate of AI tools as a metric for success.
He called the figure that over 80% of engineers use AI tools a "vanity metric," stating that what matters is the company's culture and its ability to adapt to change.
Airbnb, Inc. "Q4 2025 Earnings Call" Corrected Transcript
The role of humans is also beginning to change.
CEO Chesky stated that Airbnb "must move at the speed of AI," indicating that management roles focused solely on overseeing people will not be as necessary as they once were. He also mentioned that design and engineering managers are returning to hands-on coding work.
Investing.com "Earnings call transcript: Airbnb Q1 2026 misses EPS but beats revenue"
CTO Al-Dahle goes even further.

Airbnb operates as a global marketplace that connects travelers with hosts offering unique stays and experiences in over 220 countries and regions. By facilitating over 9 million active listings without owning the underlying real estate, the company maintains an asset-light model. This approach has allowed it to become a significant presence among travel and tourism stocks.

Management must also navigate potential risks from AI development and operational hurdles related to global expansion.

Airbnb (ABNB +0.84%) has mostly been a disappointment for investors after initially surging out of the gate in its 2020 IPO, but in 2026, the stock is finally gaining momentum.
The #1 home-sharing platform has delivered better-than-expected growth, solid margins, and it's leveraging AI to improve user satisfaction. Meanwhile, it is expanding its platform with expanded experiences and guest services offerings.
Over the last two weeks, the stock is up 9.4%, even as the S&P 500 has fallen 1.6%, as the chart below shows.
Airbnb's gains have come as the tech sector has tumbled on concerns about an AI bubble and rising interest rates. However, the company has demonstrated its resilience and is well-positioned to thrive in such an environment. Here are three reasons why Airbnb is poised to be a winner in today's stock market.
Image source: Getty Images.
Stock investors generally dislike rising interest rates. After all, higher interest rates tend to make the bond market more attractive, leading investors to rotate out of stocks and into bonds. Additionally, higher interest rates put pressure on high-priced stocks like much of the tech sector, as it makes future earnings less valuable due to a higher discount rate in the discounted cash flow.
Normally, a company like Airbnb would be susceptible to that pressure, but the home-sharing leader actually earns significant profit from interest income thanks to the funds it holds in between customer bookings and disbursement. Through the first half of the year, it's earned $363 million in interest income, more than a third of its before-tax profit, and that number is likely to go up as interest rates go up. As of the end of the second quarter, the company held $12.2 billion in "funds receivable and amounts held on behalf of customers," on which it earns interest. That's a substantial advantage of its business model and gives it resilience when many of its tech stock peers are falling in the face of higher interest rates.
The launch of Meta Platforms' Muse also exposed a hidden advantage of Airbnb. Unlike its online travel agency (OTA) rivals Expedia and Booking, Airbnb's inventory is mostly specific to its platform. Expedia and Booking, on the other hand, are essentially middlemen, connecting users to hotels and acting as a clearinghouse for hotels that want to get their listings in front of prospective customers.
Tools like Muse make it easy for users to book directly with a given hotel or with the platform that offers the lowest price. It eliminates the friction that might ordinarily lead users to book directly on Expedia and Booking. Airbnb doesn't have this problem, as homestays don't typically offer the option of booking directly. That's one of the benefits Airbnb provides to its hosts, and it should give it an advantage if users continue to adopt AI agents.

While other discretionary sectors struggle, Airbnb and its travel stock peers have continued to deliver solid growth. Despite concerns about inflation, stock and home values remain at all-time highs, enabling wealthier people to spend on vacations and travel.
A number of other factors support that trend, including record wealth among the baby boomer generation and a preference for spending money on experiences over things among younger adults. Additionally, social media has helped stoke wanderlust, and the pandemic may have convinced people to travel while they have the opportunity.
Those tailwinds might not be permanent for Airbnb, but the current strength of the travel sector shows its advantages over other consumer-facing industries.
Taken together, those three factors make the stock a good bet to continue outperforming.

Q: I booked an Airbnb rental in Toronto for a stay of more than two months. The listing description used the words “quiet” and “peaceful” five times, which was exactly what I needed for my stay.
Unfortunately, the reality was anything but calm. Almost every night, recurring heavy impact noise from the unit above would wake us up at 4 a.m. I didn’t just complain; I documented the disturbance with video and audio recordings. I shared these with the host multiple times, and while they acknowledged the ongoing noise, they couldn’t stop it.
I also reported the issue to Airbnb within the required 72-hour window. An agent reviewed my evidence and confirmed I was covered by Airbnb’s AirCover guarantee. He gave me a written commitment for a full refund of 12 unused nights and a 30% refund for the 20 nights we endured the noise. He even told me he was “currently processing” the request.
Since we moved out, Airbnb reassigned the file to multiple agents who all contradicted each other. One agent denied our eligibility entirely. Another senior manager claimed the host wasn’t willing to alter the dates, despite the thread showing the host had already approved the early checkout. The agent then tried to close the case without giving us a cent.
I just want Airbnb to honor the written commitment its agent made. Can you help me get them to pay what they promised?
— Tatsuyuki Morishita, North York, Ontario
A: Airbnb should have stuck to its word. When an agent confirms AirCover eligibility and provides a specific refund amount in writing, that’s a contract. You relied on that commitment when you packed your bags and left. For the company to play “hot potato” with your case afterward is unacceptable.
AirCover is supposed to protect guests when a listing isn’t what was advertised. Since “quiet” was a central feature of the description, the early-morning noise brigade was a clear violation.
You documented the noise, notified the host and got a promise from support before you left the premises. Good job! Many travelers make the mistake of leaving first and asking for money later, but you had the “green light” in writing.
When a company goes silent or starts walking back a promise, you should appeal to an executive. I list the names and email addresses of Airbnb’s leadership on my advocacy site, Elliott.org.
I contacted Airbnb on your behalf. Shortly after that, a member of the senior support team called you. While you rightly insisted on keeping the conversation in writing, they followed up on the platform to apologize. Airbnb honored the original refund of $1,268 and even threw in a $250 coupon for the trouble.

Utah police raided an Airbnb with guns drawn over stolen Legos, found nothing — and taxpayers will pay for it
Mon, October 19, 2026 at 5:00 PM CDT 6 min read
gettyimages.com / Michael Blackshire (left); youtube.com / Reckless Ben (right)
On March 11, 2026, Utah cops with guns drawn, including an assault rifle, made their way into an Airbnb, executing a search warrant for "stolen Legos." They detained all of the occupants, including a 16-year-old minor, and took them down to the American Fork Police Department (AFPD) station for questioning. The cops found no stolen Legos, drugs or weapons in the Airbnb.
"This is how people can end up getting killed," attorney Solomon Radner said in a press conference. "This is not how a search warrant is supposed to go down, especially if you're dealing with people whose only crime, supposedly, is stolen Legos."

About seven months later, four of the arrested occupants — Sheldon Norcross, Tyler Shaw, Sierra Lauts and Steven Allen — filed a federal civil rights lawsuit against the city of American Fork and 13 of its police officers, according to a report by The Salt Lake Tribune. They alleged that their First and Fourth Amendment rights were violated during the encounter, according to local news outlet KSL.
The lawsuit included 19 counts that were supported by incriminating records taken from the officers' equipment –– including bodycam and dashcam footage. The plaintiffs, in the opinion of their legal counsel, were repeatedly targeted by American Fork officers without legal justification.
During one roadside stop before the Airbnb arrests, one officer was caught on camera saying, "I was gonna scare him a little bit and let him go, is all I really was gonna do."
While the lawsuit against American Fork is just beginning, much of the actual dispute that started everything has been settled. Because of the nature of the lawsuit, however, if the city loses or settles, the local taxpayers will be the ones who foot the bill.
The Lego collection that led to an armed raid and arrests
The story began with a prized Star Wars Lego collection that belonged to an elderly Oregon man, Ed Mansell, and his son Bryan. They had consigned the collection — which is allegedly worth $80,000, including an ultra-rare Cloud City set valued as high as $10,000 — at an Oregon store branch of Bricks & Minifigs.
The collection vanished between corporate transfers and ownership changes, leaving the family unpaid, according to Courthouse News.
In a bid to recover their collection, the family reached out to Ben Schneider, a Los Angeles YouTuber known as Reckless Ben, whose channel digs into disputes like this one. He offered to help and, together with some local helpers, traveled to American Fork to film a documentary, file lawsuits and serve court papers to an individual connected to the missing Legos.
Schneider, who has 2.6 million YouTube subscribers, posted a video called "I tracked down the thief who stole $200,000 of LEGO."
But Schneider and his helpers ended up with four days of traffic stops, searches and, finally, the raid that landed them all in police questioning.
While none of the four individuals who filed the civil rights lawsuit were ever charged with any crime, Schneider himself faced criminal charges for stalking and residential picketing, according to a news report by ABC4 Utah.
